text: You get a string of digits from two to nine. Each digit maps to letters, like on an old phone keypad. Return every letter combination the number could spell.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — I pick one letter for each digit, in the same order as the digits, so every answer has the same length as the input. And the keypad is the usual one: two is a b c, seven is p q r s, nine is w x y z, and one has no letters. Is that right?
Yes. You can return them in any order.
Got it. Are there any constraints on the input size? And can the input be empty?
The length is between one and four, and every digit is from two to nine. So no, it's never empty.

Okay. Four digits is tiny. Each digit has three or four letters, so the biggest answer is four to the fourth, two hundred fifty-six strings. The question asks for all of them, so an exponential output is expected. Quick check on the example, two three. Two gives a b c, three gives d e f. Pair every first letter with every second letter: a d, a e, a f, through c f. That's three times three, nine. And two alone gives a, b, c.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would write one nested loop per digit. But the number of digits isn't fixed, so I can't hard-code the loops. This problem reminds me of backtracking on a decision tree. Each digit is one level of the tree. At level i, I try each letter of that digit, then go one level down. When I've used every digit, the path from the root is one answer. Recursion gives me a loop per digit, for any length.

Here's the plan. One: keep a small table, indexed by the digit's value — ten entries, and the first two are empty. Two: when i reaches the length, every digit has a letter, so save the string. Three: for each letter of digit i, recurse with the string plus that letter, and i plus one. One thing worth flagging — I pass the string by value, and build the child's string with res plus c. The child gets a new string; my own copy never changes. So there's no undo step: when the loop moves from a to b, the prefix is still clean. There's a trade-off: by reference with push back and pop back is also correct and avoids the copies, but by value is simpler and harder to get wrong. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The search either saves the finished string or loops over the letters of the current digit, passing res plus c down. Digits at i minus the character zero turns the character two into the number two, so index two really is a b c. If I dropped the two empty entries but kept minus zero, two would give g h i, and eight or nine would read past the end. One thing worth flagging — the return in the base case matters. Without it, the code would read the null character past the end and index the table at minus forty-eight. That's undefined behavior.

Let's dry-run the code with two three. Expected: a d through c f, nine strings. The key moment is when the whole a branch is done: the top call moves on to b, and its own res is still empty, because res plus c never touched it. No cleanup was needed. Thirteen calls, nine answers, in the expected order. Corner cases: two gives a, b, c in four calls. Seven needs the entry p q r s, not p q r. Two two two two is the smallest at length four, eighty-one answers. And an empty input returns one empty string; it's not allowed now, but older versions expected an empty list, so I'd add one defensive line.

Let me think about complexity here. The worst case is every digit a seven or a nine, the only keys with four letters. For seven nine seven nine, that's two hundred fifty-six answers from three hundred forty-one calls, and the output is one thousand twenty-four characters. Time is four to the n times n: up to four to the n answers, and building and saving each one costs linear time. The inner calls are fewer than the leaf calls, so they don't change the bound, and I can't beat the output size. Space is linear recursion depth, not counting the output. Strictly, each frame keeps its own copy of res, so it's n squared characters on the stack, but with n at most four, that's nothing.
You said by value means no undo. What if someone optimizes it to a reference?

Good question. With a reference, they must add the undo. The correct form is push back, recurse, pop back, and that passes all four thousand six hundred eighty legal inputs. The bug is to mutate without undo, like res plus-equals c with no pop back. Then the old letter stays: on two, you get a, a b, a b c, instead of a, b, c. It fails every legal input. The same thing happens even by value if you write plus-equals inside the loop. And the reference version is faster: on seven nine seven nine, nine point eight nine microseconds by value versus four point five eight by reference, about two times. At this size both are tiny, so I'd keep by value for clarity, and switch only in a hot loop.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You explained why res plus c by value needs no undo, and showed it in the trace with the top call still holding an empty string. You knew exactly what breaks with a reference and no pop back. And you tied the cost to the output, backed by real numbers. Catching the empty-input case was a nice touch too. Good work.
